## Prereqs

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
library(rvest)
library(corrplot)
library(mda.biber)
library(polars)
```

## Intro

This pipeline describes the process of completing the analysis. See the [Santa Barbara Pipeline](santa_barbara_pipeline.md) and the [Scraps from the Loft Pipeline](scraps_from_loft_pipeline.md) for information on how the component data frames were assembled and where the data came from. 

This document is used to describe how the individual data frames were combined, the shape of the resulting data frame, and the steps of the analysis. Final results and exploration of the analysis is documented in the [Dramaticity Analysis](dramaticity_analysis.md) document. 

## Creating all_transcripts df

First, we load in the tv_show_transcripts pipeline as a csv (saved to avoid repeated webscraping).

```{r}
#| output: false

tv_show_df <- read.csv("private/tv_show_transcripts.csv")

tv_show_df
```


Then, we can recreate the SB data frame with the code described in the [Santa Barabara Pipeline](santa_barbara_pipeline.md). Since this file can't be shared, we can just read it in below. 

```{r}
#| output: false

sb_files <- read.csv("private/sb_files.csv")

sb_files
```





Finally, we combine the two data frames.

```{r}
#| output: false

all_transcripts <- rbind(sb_files, tv_show_df)

all_transcripts
```


## Summary all_transcripts

Below is some summary information about what is included in all_transcripts:

Number of rows and columns in our df

```{r}
nrow(all_transcripts)
ncol(all_transcripts)
```

Approximate number of words in our df:

```{r}
all_transcripts |>
  mutate(nwords = (str_count(clean_words, "\\w+"))) |>
  summarize(sum(nwords))
```

Approximate number of words by category:

```{r}
all_transcripts |>
  mutate(id = if_else(str_detect(id, "transcript"), str_extract(id, "transcript"), str_extract(id, "trn"))) |>
  mutate(nwords = (str_count(clean_words, "\\w+"))) |>
  group_by(id) |>
  summarize(sum(nwords))
```

## Tagging all_transcripts

Tagging the transcripts required a python package. This process was completed in an ipynb file which will be embedded for reference below.  

```{python}
#spacy word parsing
import spacy
#pybiber
import pybiber as pb
#polars data frames
import polars as pl
```

```{python}
nlp = spacy.load("en_core_web_sm", disable=["ner"])
```

```{python}
#loading our df
all_transcripts = pl.read_csv("private/all_transcripts.csv")
```

```{python}
#checking to see if we got the right df
all_transcripts.head()
```
```{python}
processor = pb.CorpusProcessor()
df_dramaticity = processor.process_corpus(all_transcripts, nlp_model=nlp)
```

```{python}
df_biber_dramaticity = pb.biber(df_dramaticity)
```

```{python}
print(f"Matrix dimensions: {df_biber_dramaticity.shape}")
df_biber_dramaticity.head()
```

```{python}
df_biber_dramaticity.write_csv("private/df_biber_dramaticity")
```


## Getting 67 Features

Now, we can move that file back into R. As can b seen at the end of the notebook, we write out a new csv file that contains the tagged words. These can now be run through the process to get the 67 linguistic features. 

```{r}
#| output: false

#reads in the csv file created in the notebook
df_biber_dramaticity <- read.csv("private/df_biber_dramaticity")
```


Once read in, the process described [here](https://cran.r-project.org/web/packages/mda.biber/vignettes/introduction.html) is used to run our first attempt at the mda. 

It is worth noting that at this point, this is more of a test analysis in order to get a better idea of how the process works and be able to work backwards to understand how to improve the process.

```{r}
#| output: false

#ok so first we are assigning our data set to the variable d
d <- df_biber_dramaticity %>%
  #then, we are modifying a column called doc_id to extract strings that are either transcript or trn for their respective data sources
  mutate(doc_id = if_else(str_detect(doc_id, "transcript"), str_extract(doc_id, "transcript"), str_extract(doc_id, "trn"))) %>%
  #then we are modifying our new column so the strings are factors
  mutate(doc_id = as.factor(doc_id)) %>%
  #this is identifying only the columns that aren't 0?
  select(where(~ any(. != 0)))
```

This changes the labels of the id column so that our groups are formed, turns them into factors, and removes any columns with 0 instances. 

```{r}
screeplot_mda(d)
```
A screeplot is used to determine the dimensions we want to keep in our analysis. The 'elbow' is determined by AF. Anything at or below the elbow is considered 'scree' and we do not want to include that in our analysis. In this case, we should include two factors because their are two points above the AF. 

```{r}
cor_m <- cor(d[,-1], method = "pearson")

corrplot(cor_m, type = "upper", order = "hclust", tl.col = "black", tl.srt = 45, diag = F, tl.cex = 0.5)
```
This plot is a representation of correlation between features. Blue indicates positive correlation along and red indicates negative correlation. We can see that a number of these features are correlated, so an MDA analysis makes sense. 

```{r}
#now for the actual mda, factors is set equal to 2 because of the screeplot results
m <- mda_loadings(d, n_factors = 2)
```

```{r}
attributes(m)$group_means
```

```{r}
#values arranged in descending order for factor 1
attributes(m)$loadings %>% arrange(-Factor1)
```

```{r}
stickplot_mda(m, n_factor = 1)
```
Not a very exciting graph with only a binary comparison!

```{r}
heatmap_mda(m, n_factor = 1)
```

This is a bit more telling. Interesting that emphatics appear to predict natural discourse here when compared to TV show dialogue. I hypothesized it might be the opposite. 

```{r}
boxplot_mda(m, n_factor = 1)
```

Last graph. Similar to the last one, this is just a measure of how different these document types are. Worth noting that the natural discourses varied a **lot** more and had several outliers.
